history: Comboio is a word that only Portugal uses for a train, and that a Brazilian may not expect. It is French convoi, ‘convoy’, a line of vehicles travelling together, from a verb meaning ‘to go along the way with someone’. When railways arrived in the nineteenth century, a row of carriages pulled by an engine looked like a convoy, and in Portugal the name stuck. Brazil borrowed train instead and says trem. So in Portugal you go to the estação de comboios, buy a bilhete and check the linha, the platform. English convoy is the same French word, still meaning a column of ships or trucks.
historyEinfach: Comboio means ‘train’ in Portugal. The word comes from French convoi, ‘convoy’: vehicles that travel together. A train is many carriages that travel together. In Brazil people say trem, a borrowing of train.

elsewhere.text: In French, a convoi is still a convoy, and a train is a train.
Brazil borrowed the word train; Portugal took the French image of a convoy.
